## Matrix Decompositions

A **matrix decomposition** (or factorisation) writes a matrix as a product of
simpler matrices, such as triangular, orthogonal or diagonal ones. Each is used
to solve systems, compute inverses or determinants, or reveal structure.

| Decomposition | Form | Applies to | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| LU | $A=LU$ ($L$ lower, $U$ upper triangular, up to row permutation) | square matrices | solving $A\vec{x}=\vec{b}$ by Gaussian elimination |
| QR | $A=QR$ ($Q$ orthonormal columns, $R$ upper triangular) | any $A\in M_{n\times m}$, $n\geq m$ | least squares, via Gram-Schmidt |
| Cholesky | $A=LL^\top$ | symmetric positive definite | solving systems, simulating correlated Gaussians, see [[cholesky-decomposition]] |
| Spectral | $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ | symmetric | diagonalisation, quadratic forms |
| SVD | $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ | any matrix | rank, low-rank approximation, pseudoinverse |

## Spectral Decomposition

:::{.theorem data-title="Spectral Theorem"}

If $A\in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ is symmetric then there is an orthogonal matrix $Q$ and a
diagonal matrix $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ with real
entries such that
$$
A=Q\Lambda Q^\top.
$$
The columns of $Q$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A$.

:::

*Proof outline.* A symmetric matrix has a real eigenvalue $\lambda$ with unit
eigenvector $\vec{q}$ (the maximum of $\vec{x}^\top A\vec{x}$ on the unit sphere).
The subspace $\vec{q}^\perp$ is invariant under $A$ since
$\langle A\vec{x},\vec{q}\rangle=\langle\vec{x},A\vec{q}\rangle=0$ for
$\vec{x}\perp\vec{q}$, so we can repeat the argument on it by induction.

Consequences: $A$ is positive definite if and only if all $\lambda_i>0$, and
$\operatorname{Tr}(A)=\sum\lambda_i$, $\det(A)=\prod\lambda_i$. See also
[[eigenvectors]].

## Singular Value Decomposition

Every $A\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb{R})$ factors as $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ with $U,V$
orthogonal and $\Sigma$ diagonal (rectangular) with nonnegative **singular
values** $\sigma_1\geq\sigma_2\geq\cdots\geq0$, where $\sigma_i^2$ are the
eigenvalues of $A^\top A$. The number of nonzero singular values is
$\operatorname{rank}(A)$.
